![security-high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-high-priority.svg) ![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

The administrative endpoints for triggering model training (e.g., `/admin/train/batting` and `/admin/train/bowling`) lack any form of authentication or authorization beyond a global `ENABLE_HOT_RELOAD` check. When this flag is enabled, these endpoints are exposed without protection. Given that the service is configured to expose port 8000 in `docker-compose.yml`, any user with network access to the service can trigger resource-intensive training jobs, leading to potential Denial of Service or unauthorized state changes. 

Implement a robust authentication mechanism (e.g., API key validation) for all administrative endpoints.

![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

This line is vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) / Request Parameter Injection. The `cutoff_iso` and `format_code` parameters are concatenated into the URL string without proper escaping. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary query parameters into the request made to the internal `go-app` service, especially since these values can be influenced by user input via the `ml-service` API. Additionally, this lack of encoding can cause issues if `format_code` or `cutoff_iso` contain reserved characters. To remediate, use `urllib.parse.quote` to escape all user-controlled parameters before concatenating them into the URL. Remember to add `import urllib.parse` to the file. This pattern should also be updated in other training scripts (`train_bowling.py`, `train_fielding.py`, etc.).

```suggestion
    url = f"{base}/api/backtest/training-data?format={urllib.parse.quote(format_code)}&cutoff={urllib.parse.quote(cutoff_iso)}"
```

![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The `cutoff_iso` and `format_code` parameters are concatenated into the URL without escaping, allowing for request parameter injection into the internal API call to `go-app`. This pattern is consistent across multiple training scripts and should be fixed by using proper URL parameter encoding.

```suggestion
    url = f"{base}/api/backtest/training-data?format={urllib.parse.quote(format_code)}&cutoff={urllib.parse.quote(cutoff_iso)}"
```

![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The `GO_APP_API_KEY` is passed to the training subprocess as a command-line argument (`--api-key`). Command-line arguments are often visible to other users and processes on the same system (e.g., via `ps` or `/proc`). This can lead to the exposure of sensitive credentials. 

Since the subprocess inherits the environment variables of the parent process, and the training scripts are already configured to read `GO_APP_API_KEY` from the environment by default, you should remove the explicit passing of the API key as a command-line argument.

```suggestion
        extra = ["--from-api", "--cutoff", cutoff, "--all-formats", "--go-app-url", go_app_url]
```

Increasing the row count cap to 500,000 can significantly degrade the performance of the ops status dashboard when multiple large export files are present, as it requires reading up to 500k lines per file on every request. Consider a lower cap (e.g., 100,000) or caching the row counts to maintain dashboard responsiveness.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Since the derived context from `errgroup.WithContext` is explicitly ignored to prevent cascading cancellations on individual export failures, it is cleaner and more idiomatic to use a zero-valued `errgroup.Group`. The parent `ctx` (already captured as `parentCtx`) ensures goroutines still respect overall cancellation.

```suggestion
		var g errgroup.Group
```

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

This logic incorrectly calculates the win probability when the model was trained on a single class (e.g., a small format-specific dataset where only one team won all matches). In the single-class case, `proba.ravel()` returns `1.0` for that class. If the only class present was `0` (loss), the probability of winning (class `1`) should be `0.0`, but this code would return `1.0`. You should check `model.classes_` to determine which class the probability refers to.

```python
        proba = model.predict_proba(X)
        if proba.shape[1] > 1:
            p_team1 = proba[:, 1]
        else:
            # Handle single-class training data: check if the class is 1 (win) or 0 (loss)
            p_team1 = proba.ravel() if model.classes_[0] == 1 else 1.0 - proba.ravel()
        return [WinPrediction(team1_win_probability=float(p)) for p in p_team1]
```

![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The new prediction endpoint `/predict/extras` accepts a list of features without any limit on the number of items. An attacker could send an extremely large JSON array, causing the service to consume excessive memory during parsing (by Pydantic) and processing (by NumPy), potentially leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) via memory exhaustion. It is recommended to implement a maximum batch size for this endpoint.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The `TimeSeriesSplit` will raise a `ValueError` if `n_samples` is less than 3 because it requires `n_samples >= n_splits + 1`. With `max(2, ...)` ensuring at least 2 splits, any dataset with 2 or fewer samples will cause a crash during auto-tuning. While auto-tuning on such small data is unlikely, a guard or fallback to `KFold` (which also has sample requirements but is more flexible with shuffling) would improve robustness.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

These correlated subqueries for player aggregates are executed for every match in the export. While correct for avoiding data leakage, this O(N*M) approach (matches * players) can be extremely slow for large datasets. The increase of `export_timeout_ms` to 1 hour indicates this is a long-running task. If this export is triggered by an HTTP handler, it should be moved to a background job to prevent request timeouts. Additionally, `export_timeout_ms` should be a configurable parameter rather than a hardcoded value. Consider optimizing this by using a `LATERAL` join or pre-calculating match-level aggregates into a temporary table to reduce the overhead of repeated snapshot lookups.

The default timeout for training subprocesses is currently hardcoded to 7 days (`604800` seconds). As a tunable parameter, this value should be configurable, ideally via environment variables, rather than being a fixed constant in the code. This extremely long duration, especially when combined with the lack of authentication on the triggering endpoints, poses a significant Denial of Service (DoS) risk. It is recommended to make this timeout configurable and reduce its default to a more reasonable value (e.g., 1-4 hours) and ensure it is strictly enforced.

![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The administrative endpoints for triggering model training (e.g., `/admin/train/batting`, `/admin/train/bowling`) are accessible without authentication when `ENABLE_HOT_RELOAD` is enabled. This PR also removes a previous docstring warning that advised protecting these endpoints with authentication at the deployment layer. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the service could trigger resource-intensive training jobs, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) or unauthorized model updates. It is highly recommended to implement application-level authentication (e.g., an API key check) for all `/admin/*` endpoints.

The new prediction endpoints `/predict/extras` and `/predict/win` lack authentication. While they include a batch size limit, they remain susceptible to abuse if the service is exposed. Consider implementing authentication for all prediction endpoints to prevent unauthorized usage and mitigate potential DoS risks.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The new query to fetch training rows for the extras model uses four correlated subqueries to calculate feature sums (`bat_consistency_sum`, `bowl_consistency_sum`, etc.). While this is logically correct, correlated subqueries can lead to performance issues, as they may be executed once for each row in the outer query. For large datasets, this could become a bottleneck.

Consider exploring alternative approaches that might be more performant, such as using Common Table Expressions (CTEs) or `LATERAL` joins to pre-aggregate the feature data. This could potentially reduce the load on the database.

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Similar to the query for extras, this query for win prediction training rows uses eight correlated subqueries to calculate team-level feature sums. This significantly increases the query complexity and could lead to performance degradation, especially with a large number of matches.

I recommend investigating ways to optimize this query. Refactoring to use Common Table Expressions (CTEs) to gather player data and then aggregating could be more efficient than running multiple correlated subqueries for each match row.

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

The use of four separate correlated subqueries to calculate `bat_consistency_sum`, `bowl_consistency_sum`, `bat_form_sum`, and `bowl_form_sum` is likely to be inefficient. Each of these subqueries is executed for every row returned by the main query, which can lead to poor performance as the number of matches grows.

A more performant approach would be to use Common Table Expressions (CTEs). You could use a CTE to find the latest snapshot for each player involved in the relevant matches, and then another CTE to aggregate these values per match. Finally, you would join the aggregated results back to the `match` table. This would significantly reduce the number of scans on the snapshot tables.

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

Similar to the extras query, this query uses eight correlated subqueries to calculate team-level consistency and form sums. This approach will be very inefficient and is unlikely to scale well with a large number of matches, as each subquery is executed for every match in the result set.

To improve performance, I recommend refactoring this to use Common Table Expressions (CTEs). You can create CTEs to first identify the players for each team in each match, then find their latest snapshots, and finally aggregate these values per team/match before joining back to the main query. This will be much more efficient.

The administrative endpoints (`/admin/reload`, `/admin/train/*`) are protected by an API key check that is skipped if the `ADMIN_API_KEY` environment variable is not set. In the provided `docker-compose.yml`, this variable is not defined, leaving these sensitive endpoints unprotected by default. An unauthorized user with network access to the ML service could trigger resource-intensive training jobs or reload artifacts, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) or potential manipulation of the machine learning models.

![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

The `KFold` cross-validator requires at least 2 splits. When `n_samples` is 2, `n_samples - 1` results in 1 split, which will cause a `ValueError` from scikit-learn. Ensure `n_splits` is at least 2.

```suggestion
            return KFold(n_splits=max(2, min(cv_splits, n_samples - 1)), shuffle=True, random_state=random_state)
```

![security-medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/security-medium-priority.svg) ![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The training subprocesses triggered via administrative endpoints lack application-level concurrency limits and use an extremely long default timeout of 7 days (defined by `DEFAULT_TRAINING_SUBPROCESS_TIMEOUT_SEC` in `ml/config.py`). Since these jobs are executed in separate threads via `asyncio.to_thread`, an attacker could exhaust system resources (CPU, memory, and the thread pool) by triggering multiple concurrent training requests, leading to a sustained Denial of Service.

The `_df_to_xy` function in `train_bowling.py` ignores the updated feature names returned by `apply_transforms`. This will lead to incorrect feature importance mapping in `train_and_save` if interactions or log transforms are applied, as the number of columns in `X` will no longer match `FEATURE_COLS`. Align this with the implementation in `train_batting.py`.

```suggestion
    if transform_config.get("add_interactions") or transform_config.get("add_log1p"):
        X, feature_names_used = apply_transforms(X_raw, list(FEATURE_COLS), transform_config, "bowling")
    else:
        X = X_raw
        feature_names_used = list(FEATURE_COLS)
    y_cols = [c for c in TARGET_COLS if c in df.columns]
    Y = df[y_cols].astype(float).values
    if "econ" in df.columns:
        econ = df["econ"].astype(float).values.reshape(-1, 1)
    else:
        runs = df.get("runs", pd.Series(np.zeros(len(df)))).astype(float).values
        balls = df.get("balls", pd.Series(np.ones(len(df)) * 6)).astype(float).values
        overs = np.where(balls > 0, balls / 6.0, 1.0)
        econ = np.where(overs > 0, runs / overs, 0.0).reshape(-1, 1)
    needed = len(TARGET_COLS)
    if Y.shape[1] < needed:
        pad = np.zeros((Y.shape[0], needed - Y.shape[1]))
        Y = np.concatenate([Y, pad], axis=1)
    Y = np.concatenate([Y, econ], axis=1)
    return X, Y, feature_names_used
```

![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

Using a raw `errgroup.Group` without a derived context means that if one export goroutine fails, the others will continue to run using the `parentCtx`. While the comment suggests this is intentional to avoid cascading failures, it also means that a single failure won't trigger an immediate return from `g.Wait()` if other exports are still in progress, potentially delaying error reporting. If the goal is to allow partial success, consider logging individual errors within the goroutines instead of relying on `errgroup` to return the first error.
